Keep track of what matters to you with tools you put together yourself, and an AI that can read them, fill them in and set them up with you.
A demo is waiting: twelve weeks in the life of Camille, to see what the app looks like once built.
The Guide is the book at the top of the home screen.
The discovery is over: getting started is yours to do in the order you like.
What comes next waits in the Guide, the book at the top of the home screen.
This tutorial begins in the demo. Reinstall it, or skip its steps there.
These tutorials use the demo: %1$s. Without it, their steps in the demo are skipped. You can reinstall it at any time from Settings › Demo.
After a look around the demo, you create a first zone and a first tool, with no AI needed.
You now have a zone and a tool to note entries in. To choose the next ones, read “The tools at a glance”, at the start of Getting started. What remains is to connect an AI.

The demo follows Camille, who is training for a half marathon. Camille sorts life into zones, one per area, and running is one of them. In each zone, Camille notes what matters with tools, sorted here into three groups: Training, Body and Analysis.

Runs is a Tracking tool. Each run is noted in it with its date and its kilometres. A figure noted this way is called an entry.\n\nTouch + to add one. The buttons under the title are shortcuts: one touch, and the entry is noted.
The run just added already shows in this chart, and counts towards the goal “Training week”. An entry is noted once and shows up wherever it counts: chart, goal, variable.
Create your own zone, under « Ungrouped »

Go back to the home screen, scroll down to the “Ungrouped” section at the very bottom, and touch its +. Give the zone a name, an icon and a short description.\n\nNot in the Demo group, which belongs to Camille. Groups of your own come later, with the gear of the home screen.

In the zone, touch the + of a section, then choose a tool type. List is the simplest. It holds things to do, shopping or tasks, ticked once done.\n\nThe configuration screen shows many settings, but only the name is required, the others already have a value. Give the list a name, then confirm at the bottom of the screen.
Add a first entry to it
Open the list, type something to do and add it, then tick it once done.\n\nTo change the list later, touch and hold its title to open its configuration.
The AI can do the same things as you in the app: read the tools, fill them in and set them up. For that, it needs an access key from an AI provider.
The AI is connected. What remains is to build tools with it.
AI providers are set up in the Settings: Claude, OpenAI, DeepSeek, or a service compatible with OpenAI\'s API, such as Ollama or LM Studio.
Set up a provider with your key
First create an API key on the provider\'s website. In the app, touch that provider, paste the key, choose a model and save.\n\nThe key stays on the phone, and the app sends it only to that provider.

Each exchange is paid to the provider, with the key, and the conversation shows what each one cost.\n\nTo spend less, the provider\'s configuration has three settings: a smaller model, less reasoning, shorter answers with the token limit. In Settings › AI limits, you also set how many calls the AI may chain on its own before handing back.
Touch the bubble to open the conversation, and ask the AI what it sees of the app. There is no need to attach anything. It already knows the zones and tools, and reads the entries it needs by itself.
Tell it about your tool with a pointer

A pointer is how you show the AI exactly what you mean.

Write a question, for example “What do you think of this list?”. Touch the crosshair under the message to add a pointer. In the “Select data” window, touch the zone, then the tool. Tick nothing, touch Confirm, then send the message.

Ticking Config or Entries would have attached that data to the message. The “Talk to the AI” chapter explains when that helps.
Every tool has the same basic configuration: its name, its icon, its shape in the zone, fields of your own. No AI needed.
You can fit a tool to the way you use it.
In a zone, press and hold a tool\'s title, for example the list made in First steps. Its configuration opens: first the General settings, the same for every tool, then those of its type. Then Next.
Change its icon and its shape

Tap the icon to pick another one, and give it a colour. The Display mode sets the size of its tile in the zone, from the smallest, Icon, to Full, which shows everything. Tap Save, then look at the zone.
Add a field of your own
Open the configuration again. Under Extra fields, add a field, for example « Shop », of the text type, and save. Then add an entry to the tool: the Shop field is in its form. Fill it in.

Three settings matter when the AI works on this tool. With Config validation by the AI and Data validation by the AI, it asks for your approval before changing the configuration or the entries. With Always send to the AI, the tool\'s entries go with every message, without it having to ask for them. The « Talk to the AI » chapter says more. Then Next.
Describe what you want to follow, and the AI creates the tools. Everything it does stays visible, and can be changed afterwards.
The AI built a tool and a variable with you. What remains is to have it work on its own, on a schedule.
The AI creates and sets up tools, adds entries and writes variables, as you would. When a piece of information is missing, it asks with a field to fill in.
Ask the AI to create a tool

In the conversation, add a pointer to the zone and describe what you want to follow, for example “a tracker of the water I drink, in glasses”. Let the AI create the tool, or the step won\'t be marked done.
Look at the tool it made
Close the conversation and open the new tool. It is a tool like any other, changed through its configuration.
A variable is a figure worked out from entries, for example the number of glasses drunk today. Ask the AI for one: “a variable with today\'s glasses”. A goal or a chart can then use it.
Choose what it must ask before doing
In Settings › AI validation, you choose what the AI must show before acting. It then waits for your approval for each change, across the whole app, in a zone, in a tool or in a single conversation.
With a routine, a message for the AI is prepared once and used again as often as you like.
The routine is ready. The AI will handle it on its schedule, and you can run it or talk it over at any time. The rest is in Getting started, to read in any order.

A routine's message serves in two ways.

The AI can handle it on its own. It reads the tools, writes in them if the message asks for it, and the result is there to read later. With a schedule, it takes care of it by itself, every Sunday evening for example.

It can also be used to start a conversation with the AI, handy for a talk that comes back often, like “let's look back on my week”.
Create a routine in a zone
A routine belongs to a zone, like a tool. In the zone, touch the + of a section, choose “Routine” and give it a name.
On the routine\'s card, touch the pencil. Write what the AI should do, for example “sum up my week”. To have it run on its own, add a schedule, such as every Sunday at 6 pm. Save.
To see what it does without waiting for its schedule, touch the play button on its card.
Each run is kept in the routine\'s history. Touch one to see what the AI read, did and answered, and what it cost.

On the same card, touch the bubble to start a conversation with the routine\'s message. It can go as it is or be changed first. This is the right choice to think things through with the AI rather than let it work alone.
Groups of zones on the home screen, groups of tools in a zone, the layout of the tiles.
Variables, readings, pointers from one entry to another.
The conversation with the AI: what you can attach, how it answers you and asks for your consent, what you set for each conversation, what it costs.
You know how to attach what is needed, answer the AI and set a conversation. Routines do the same without you: the Routines chapter.

At the top: the clock opens a past conversation again, to resume it; the square stops it (it stays in the history and can be resumed); the gear opens its settings; the cross closes the screen. Under the title, a line says what the AI is doing: thinking, reading, waiting for your answer. Then Next.
Once a conversation is stopped by the square, the bubble offers « Start a chat »: the AI starts from scratch, and keeps from one conversation to the next only what the app holds. Then Next.

Under the message, the buttons add blocks: Text, a file (the paperclip; a long file can go whole or as a preview only), a photo, an image from the gallery, and the pointer\'s target. This time, in the pointer, check Entries: the tool\'s entries go with the message, over the period and with the filters you choose. Config attaches its settings. With nothing checked, the AI only knows what you are talking about, and reads what it needs itself. Each block can be changed (pencil) or removed (bin). Ask for instance « Sum up my entries of the week », send, then Next.

It may ask you a question: pick an answer, or « Reply with a message », or « Add a note » to your choice. Before changing what you protect, it asks for your consent: « Allow » or « Refuse ». If the data it asks for goes past your threshold, the app asks whether to send it. While it works, « Interrupt » stops its round. A long press on a message copies it. Then Next.
Ask for your consent in this conversation

The gear, then « Session settings ». Under « Also ask for my approval on », check for instance « The tools\' data »: until this conversation ends, the AI will ask you before each write to a tool. It adds to the protections already set, without replacing them.

In the same settings, « Reasoning » sets for this conversation alone how much the AI thinks before answering: the more it thinks, the slower and dearer. « Costs » details what the conversation cost: what went out, what came back, what was read again from the cache. Then Next.
Themes, palettes, the colours of icons.
Plugging Claude into the app from outside, as a connector.
